meta.title_plain: How to launch your own company
meta.teaser: Turn one good idea into your very first happy customer, step by step.

page.title: How to launch your own company: from idea to first customer
page.sub: A skill you can use today
page.bigIdea: Mikaila Ulmer started selling lemonade at about age 4, and later it was in over 1,500 stores. Every big company starts the same way: one idea, one customer, then lots of practice.

cards.title: Start with a real problem
cards.front: The best ideas fix something or make people smile.
cards.back: Mikaila used her great-grandmother's 1940s lemonade recipe, sweetened with local honey. She wanted to help bees, and gives part of her profits to save them.
cards.tryit: Spend 10 minutes listing 5 small problems you notice at home, at school or on the tennis court.

cards.title: Test your idea first
cards.front: Before you build it, find out if anyone wants it.
cards.back: The U.S. Small Business Administration calls this market research. Ask real people if they need your idea. Check who already sells something similar.
cards.tryit: Ask 3 family members: "Would you use this? What would you pay?" Write down their answers.

cards.title: Make a one-page plan
cards.front: A plan is like a game strategy before a match.
cards.back: Write what you sell, who buys it, what it costs to make and your price. The price minus the cost is your profit.
cards.tryit: Pick your best idea. In 15 minutes, fill in four lines: product, customer, cost and price.

cards.title: Find your first customer
cards.front: One happy customer beats a hundred maybe-customers.
cards.back: Mikaila first sold lemonade in front of her house. Then a local pizza shop asked to sell it. Start small and close to home.
cards.tryit: Write a one-sentence offer, like "I'll teach your little brother a forehand drill." Practise saying it to Dad.

cards.title: Listen, improve, grow
cards.front: Your first version won't be perfect. That's normal.
cards.back: Feedback shows you what to fix. Mikaila's company grew step by step. In 2015 she got $60,000 from Daymond John on the TV show Shark Tank.
cards.tryit: Ask one person who tried your idea: "What's one thing I could make better?" Write it down.

words.d: A person who starts their own business or project.
A person who buys or uses what you offer.
Finding out if people want your idea before you build it.
The money left over after you pay what it cost to make.
What people tell you about your work so you can improve it.

quiz.q: What's the best way to start a company idea?
opts: Pick the most expensive product you can think of
Copy exactly what a big brand already sells
Find a problem people have, or something that makes them happy
quiz.hint: Look back at card 1. Why did Mikaila make her lemonade?
quiz.why: Companies grow when they help people, so a real problem is the best starting point.

quiz.q: You think kids at school want custom tennis grip tape. What should you do first?
opts: Ask a few kids if they'd want it and what they'd pay
Keep it secret until it's perfect
quiz.hint: What does the Small Business Administration call checking an idea first?
quiz.why: Market research tells you if people want your idea before you spend money on it.

quiz.q: You sell bracelets for 5 dollars, and each one costs 2 dollars to make. What's your profit per bracelet?
quiz.hint: Profit is what's left after you pay for making it.
quiz.why: Price minus cost is profit, so 5 minus 2 leaves 3 dollars.

quiz.q: Your first customer says your product is OK but a bit boring. What's the smart move?
opts: Use the feedback to make the next version better
quiz.hint: Think about how a coach helps you fix your serve.
quiz.why: Feedback is like coaching: it shows you exactly what to practise and improve.

page.think: Plan your own mini company. What would you sell or teach, like drawings, tennis tips for younger kids or a Roblox game you built? Who would your first customer be, and what would you ask them?
